summary: Several added comments overstate behavior that the implementation does not guarantee.

items.issue: The comment states that deserializing an enumeration yields its singleton object, but the implementation unconditionally requires the runtime subclass to expose the public Scala module field. A non-module subclass has no such field and deserialization fails instead.
items.suggestion: Qualify this as resolution for singleton-module enumerations and document the module-field assumption (or the possible failure).

items.issue: `nextId` is not guaranteed to be available: explicitly constructing values with out-of-order ids can leave `nextId` pointing at an already-used id, causing the subsequent construction to hit the duplicate-id assertion.
items.suggestion: Replace “next available integer id” with “current `nextId`” and, if useful, document that duplicate ids are rejected.

items.issue: As with the named constructor, `nextId` is not necessarily unused after out-of-order explicit-id construction, so “next available integer id” is inaccurate.
items.suggestion: Describe the id as the current `nextId`, rather than as available.

items.issue: These comments promise stable ordinary-set semantics, but `nnIds` is offset by the mutable enclosing `bottomId` at every operation. If a ValueSet is created and a later value has a lower id, existing bit positions are reinterpreted; for example, a set originally holding id 0 can subsequently iterate as id -1. The documented range, membership, update, and iteration behavior is then false.
items.suggestion: Document the required invariant that no later lower-id values are added after creating a ValueSet, or fix the representation so the offset is stable.

items.issue: The explanation says iteration begins at a value whose zero-adjusted id equals `start.id` (or at `start` with no negative ids). `iteratorFrom` instead starts at the least present bit at or above that position, so no such value need exist and `start` need not be a member of the set.
items.suggestion: State that it begins at the first present value meeting the implementation’s threshold, including the absent-start case.

bonus_findings.issue: The comment calls `topId` the highest id used, but the implementation maintains it as one greater than the highest created id (and it can equal `initial` before any value exists).
bonus_findings.suggestion: Describe it as one greater than the highest id, consistently with `maxId`’s comment.
